# 2 Kings Chapter 1 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 222r–222v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2KI_001_page_001.jpg, 2KI_001_page_002.jpg

---

## Consensus Translation

**1** Moab rebelled against Israel after the death of Ahab.

**2** Ahaziah fell through the lattice in his upper room in Samaria and was injured. He sent messengers and said to them, "Go, inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron, whether I shall recover from this injury."

**3** But the angel of the LORD spoke to Elijah the Tishbite: "Arise, go up to meet the messengers of the king of Samaria and say to them, 'Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are going to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron?'

**4** Therefore thus says the LORD: 'You shall not come down from the bed to which you have gone up, for you shall surely die.'" And Elijah departed.

**5** The messengers returned to Ahaziah, and he said to them, "Why have you returned?"

**6** They said to him, "A man came up to meet us and said to us, 'Go back to the king who sent you and tell him: Thus says the LORD — Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are sending to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron? Therefore you shall not come down from the bed to which you have gone up, for you shall surely die.'"

**7** He said to them, "What sort of man was he who came up to meet you and spoke these words to you?"

**8** They answered him, "A hairy man with a leather belt around his waist." He said, "It is Elijah the Tishbite."

**9** Then the king sent to him a captain of fifty with his fifty men. He went up to him — and there was Elijah, sitting on the top of a hill. He said to him, "Man of God, the king says, 'Come down!'"

**10** Elijah answered the captain of fifty, "If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty." Then fire came down from heaven and consumed him and his fifty.

**11** Again the king sent to him another captain of fifty with his fifty men. He said to him, "Man of God, thus says the king, 'Come down at once!'"

**12** Elijah answered them, "If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty." Then the fire of God came down from heaven and consumed him and his fifty.

**13** Again the king sent a third captain of fifty with his fifty men. The third captain of fifty went up and came and fell on his knees before Elijah and pleaded with him, "Man of God, please let my life and the lives of these fifty servants of yours be precious in your sight.

**14** Behold, fire came down from heaven and consumed the two former captains of fifty with their fifties. But now, let my life be precious in your sight."

**15** The angel of the LORD said to Elijah, "Go down with him; do not be afraid of him." So he arose and went down with him to the king.

**16** He said to him, "Thus says the LORD: 'Because you sent messengers to inquire of Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron — is it because there is no God in Israel to inquire of his word? — therefore you shall not come down from the bed to which you have gone up, for you shall surely die.'"

**17** So Ahaziah died according to the word of the LORD that Elijah had spoken. Jehoram succeeded him as king in the second year of Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, because Ahaziah had no son.

**18** Now the rest of the acts of Ahaziah that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?

---
## SOPHIA's Council Notes

All three translators recognize this chapter as a transition text bridging 1 Kings and 2 Kings. The threefold repetition of "Is there no God in Israel?" (vv.3, 6, 16) is the theological heartbeat of the chapter. The fire-from-heaven motif deliberately echoes 1 Kings 18 (Carmel), establishing Elijah's prophetic authority as the frame for his approaching departure in chapter 2. The three-captains sequence follows the folktale pattern of two failures resolved by a third who acts differently — here, through humility rather than command.

---
## Disagreement Log

### V.2 — "injured" vs. "was sick"
- **EMET:** "and-was-sick"
- **LOGOS:** "was injured"
- **PNEUMA:** "was badly injured"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "was injured" — the verb *vayechal* in context refers to injury from the fall, not illness. LOGOS captures this accurately. PNEUMA's "badly" adds interpretive emphasis.

### V.8 — "hairy man" vs. "garment of hair"
- **EMET:** "a-possessor of-hair [ba'al se'ar]"
- **LOGOS:** "A hairy man"
- **PNEUMA:** "He wore a garment of hair"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "A hairy man" — the Hebrew *ba'al se'ar* most naturally reads as a description of the person. PNEUMA's interpretation (garment) is plausible but goes beyond the text.

### V.9 — "mountain" vs. "hill"
- **EMET:** "the-top of-the-mountain"
- **LOGOS:** "the top of a hill"
- **PNEUMA:** "top of a hill"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "the top of a hill" — *har* can mean either; the military context favors "hill," though the theological echoes of Sinai/Carmel are noted.

### V.11 — "quickly" / "at once" / "immediately"
- **EMET:** "quickly [meherah]"
- **LOGOS:** "at once"
- **PNEUMA:** "immediately"
- **SOPHIA ruling:** "at once" — all three capture the urgency of *meherah*; LOGOS is most concise.

---
*— SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
